newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal investment funds admit switch to shares.
newsitem.headline: Portugal investment funds admit switch to shares.

text.p: Portuguese investment funds, traditionally wary of the stock market, admit to having had a change of heart in 1997, saying they have been behind some 30 percent of business on the surging Lisbon bourse.

"I should think the level of business involving the funds must be pretty close to 30 percent", Jose Carlos Maia, president of the Portuguese Association of Investment Fund Management and a board member at the Caixagest fund, told Reuters.

Traders point to the relative good health of the Portuguese economy, the encouraging corporate profit outlook, the strengthening of pension funds and the growing interest of foreign investors as lying behind stock market optimism.
But probably the key factor has been the decline in interest rates which has made the bond market a less attractive alternative for the big funds.
The PSI20 .PSI20 index has risen some 10 percent in the first eight sessions of the year after gaining over 30 percent in 1996 when it was Europe's fourth-highest performer.
Raul Marques, manager at Tottafundos which has some 30 billion escudos in the stock market, did not see the market's gain as exaggerated, although he said that there was a need for caution.

"A year ago, the market was pretty cheap, but, at the moment the price/earnings ration for 1997 is not far from 15 and the price/cashflow a little above six, which are not extraordinary numbers in international terms," he said.

Manuel Puerta da Costa, a deputy director at Banco Portugues de Investimento, considered the "January" effect -- the surge both in prices and volumes at the start of the year -- to be normal, reflecting confidence about the rest of the year.
"The January effect comes about because many funds prefer not to invest at the end of a year and make their move at the beginning of the next so as not to hurt their profitability," he said.
Raul Marques said that the situation on the capital markets at the moment was exceptionally good.

"The international outlook is good. The dollar is strong and inflation is under control. All the latest American and European indicators have been positive...the situation is exceptionally good," he said.
Puerta da Costa said that Portugal was seen as somehere between an emerging market and a small European (stock) market.
"The switch from one (emerging) to the other (small European) still has not fully happened," he said.

But when it does, analysts say, it will have an immense impact on liquidity as foreign funds, particularly American, will automatically either boost or start to have weightings in the Portuguese market.
Despite the sharp gains at the start of the year, fund managers were confident that the advance was solid.

"Any correction (in prices)...will be a good opportunity to buy," said Puerta da Costa, adding that the domestic market would only suffer a serious correction if there were a sharp setback in foreign bourses.
